newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lower German cocoa grind could be permanent.
newsitem.headline: Lower German cocoa grind could be permanent.

text.p: Lower 1996 German cocoa grindings reflect a concentration in processing capacity elsewhere and may well be here to stay, Karsten Keunecke, managing director of confectionery industry BDS said.

"Plants in Berlin have been shut and internationally operating companies have moved capacity to Belgium, France and the Netherlands," he said in response to questions during a press conference ahead of the ISM confectionery trade fair.
"That's normal within the single European market and it makes sense."
Keunecke said the concentration of processing was part of a worldwide trend in the cocoa industry.
This also brought higher grindings capacity at origin and mergers and takeovers in global manufacturing and trading.
The German grind in 1996 dropped by three percent to 251,069 tonnes.
This was well down from more than 300,000 tonnes seen in the early 1990s, when chocolate production boomed amid emerging eastern German demand.
Keunecke said the number of firms reporting to BDS -- which process beans into cocoa liquor and mass -- had fallen to 17 from 27 ten years ago.
But the grind figure did not document lower chocolate demand.
Domestic sales of chocolate and sweets were up one percent from 1995's 2.44 million tonnes last year, market research showed.
